declared.title: The Moderating Effect of Individual Differences in Error-Management Training
declared.foundIn: Crossref search « error encouragement error avoidance training transfer control training Human Factors » (2026-11-26); named by the counter-evidence review

population: 164 trainees randomly allocated to error-encouragement, error-avoidance or neutral instructions on a simulated air traffic control task

findings.text: Training that encouraged errors gave better transfer than training that told people to avoid errors, but no better than a neutral training

support.sentence: Error encouragement yielded better transfer performance than did error avoidance but was no better than the control training.

findings.text: Trainees of higher ability benefited more from training focused on errors than trainees of lower ability

support.sentence: Higher- rather than lower-ability trainees benefited from training with an error orientation (positive or negative), suggesting that learning from errors in training requires greater cognitive resources.

findings.text: Telling trainees to avoid errors harmed them, especially the less open, less agreeable and lower-ability ones

support.sentence: Error-avoidance training had a detrimental effect especially for those less open to experience, lower in agreeableness, and of lower ability.

limits: one simulated task (air traffic control), one study; country not given in the abstract
the authors attribute earlier benefits of error encouragement to confounds (active exploration, task information), which they controlled here
transfer measured after a short training, not real work
